clinicalPearls: NSGCT includes embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, frequently occurring together as a mixed germ cell tumour, and tends to present at a younger age than seminoma
AFP and/or beta-hCG are elevated in most non-seminomatous tumours: yolk sac elements raise AFP and choriocarcinoma or trophoblastic elements raise beta-hCG, while LDH reflects tumour bulk
Any germ cell tumour with a raised AFP is treated as NSGCT, even when the resected specimen appears to be pure seminoma
Radical inguinal orchidectomy provides diagnosis and local control, and post-orchidectomy marker decline is used to define the risk group
Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection has a role in selected patients, and cisplatin-based chemotherapy is central to management of metastatic disease
Post-chemotherapy residual masses may contain viable tumour or mature teratoma and often require surgical resection because teratoma is chemoresistant and can grow or transform
Sperm banking should be offered before orchidectomy, chemotherapy, or retroperitoneal surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ but differentiate along embryonic and extra-embryonic lines. Embryonal carcinoma represents primitive undifferentiated cells, yolk sac tumour produces AFP, choriocarcinoma comprises cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast that secrete beta-hCG with a marked propensity for early haematogenous spread, and teratoma contains somatic tissues derived from multiple germ layers. Most tumours are mixed. Isochromosome 12p is characteristic. Lymphatic spread to the retroperitoneum predominates, but choriocarcinoma disseminates early through the bloodstream to lung, liver, and brain.
additionalDifferentials: Burned-out germ cell tumour presenting with metastases and a testicular scar
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to confirm an intratesticular solid lesion
Serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH before and serially after orchidectomy
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for staging, with brain imaging if choriocarcinoma or neurological features
Semen analysis and sperm banking before treatment
Imaging and marker reassessment of residual masses after chemotherapy to guide resection
redFlags: Very high beta-hCG with widespread visceral or cerebral metastases from choriocarcinoma
Haemoptysis or acute respiratory compromise from pulmonary metastases
Markers failing to normalise or rising after orchidectomy
Enlarging residual retroperitoneal mass after chemotherapy suggesting teratoma or viable tumour
Neurological deterioration suggesting brain metastases or haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: With stage-appropriate surgery and cisplatin-based chemotherapy the majority of patients with NSGCT are cured, including many with metastatic disease; prognosis is stratified by marker levels and metastatic sites, being least favourable with markedly elevated markers and non-pulmonary visceral metastases.
pitfalls: Managing a marker-positive tumour as seminoma when a raised AFP mandates NSGCT treatment
Assuming a shrinking post-chemotherapy mass needs no surgery when residual teratoma is chemoresistant
Omitting sperm banking before gonadotoxic therapy
Underestimating the early haematogenous spread of choriocarcinoma
